catalog_quote: The East Bodish languages Kurtöp, Bumthang, Khengkha, Dakpa, Dzala and Chali share a tonal system which exhibits less contrasts than the Central Bodish languages. ... Data from Kurtöp and Dakpa will be used to illustrate the East Bodish tone system, which is characterized as follows. Tone (high/low) is contrastive on the first syllable of words, following sonorant consonants. Unlike in Dzongkha, there does not appear to be salient glottalization concomitant with high tone. Although long vowels do contrast, at least in some dialects of Kurtöp, there are contrasts of short versus long vowels in open syllables, in addition to the tonal contrast. Following obstruents, tone is not contrastive but instead predictable. As shown in Hyslop (2009), high tone follows voiceless initials and low tone follows voiced initials. ... An identical system is found in Dakpa, Chali, Dzala, Bumthap and Khengkha. Some Dakpa data also show this contrast in (12-15) below. To date, no East Bodish languages have been found with a system similar to Dzongkha; that is, I have come across no East Bodish language contrasting a tonal contour or a high/low tonal contrast following obstruents in addition to a voicing contrast on the obstruent.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (+, lines 6138-6167) opened. Hyslop 2010, sec. 2.3 'East Bodish tonal system', printed p. 117 = p. 124 (verified with extracted text): every segment of the reported quote is there word for word ('The East Bodish languages Kurtöp, Bumthang, Khengkha, Dakpa, Dzala and Chali share a tonal system which exhibits less contrasts than the Central Bodish languages.'.. 'Tone (high/low) is contrastive on the first syllable of words, following sonorant consonants. Unlike in Dzongkha, there does not appear to be salient glottalization concomitant with high tone.'.. 'Following obstruents, tone is not contrastive but instead predictable. As shown in Hyslop (2009), high tone follows voiceless initials…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dzala is described as having the common East Bodish word-tone system: a binary high/low register tone realised on the first syllable of the word, lexically contrastive only after sonorant onsets and predictable after obstruents (high after voiceless, low after voiced). No source opened says where stress falls or whether Dzala has word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the palatal fricative (voiceless only) contrasts high vs low tone after an obstruent (stated for Kurtöp). For the Cuona/Mama variety, Lu 2002 p. 48 (snippet) reports a light/neutral tone confined to word-final syllables and Namkung 1996 p. 83 a low-falling tone confined to grammatical particles.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain for tone: contrast located on the first syllable of (citation-form) words; the Dzala claim is a generalisation from the author's East Bodish field notes, illustrated with Kurtöp and Dakpa forms rather than Dzala forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Hyslop 2010) concerns Dzala as spoken in Trashi'yangtse/Lhuntse, NE Bhutan = dzal1238 proper (her own East Bodish field notes; Dzala said to be 'identical' to the Kurtöp/Dakpa system she illustrates). The Glottolog-listed primary descriptions (Lu Shaozun 1986 Cuona Menbayu jianzhi; Lu 2002; Sun et al. 1980) describe the Mama-township variety of Lebu district, Cuona county, Tibet: van Driem (2001: 914-915; 2007: 72) and Glottolog assign this 'southern dialect' to Dzala, but Bodt (2023: 70-73, Bulletin of Tibetology 54.1) treats it as a Dakpa variety (DkM), i.e. closer to dakp1242; Namkung 1996's 'Cuona (Southern/Mama)' entry is that same variety. Lu's 'northern dialect' (Wenlang/Bangxin, Motuo) is Tshangla per van Driem but Dakpa per Bodt. Kurtöp (kurt1248) stress facts from Hyslop 2011 are sister-language context only.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 2.3 p. 117: East Bodish (Kurtöp, Bumthang, Khengkha, Dakpa, Dzala, Chali) share one tonal system: high/low tone contrastive on the first syllable of words after sonorants, predictable after obstruents (high after voiceless, low after voiced); 'An identical system is found in Dakpa, Chali, Dzala, Bumthap and Khengkha.'

sources.citation: Hyslop, Gwendolyn. 2011. A grammar of Kurtöp. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon.
sources.note: Sister language only: sec. 7.2 pp. 186-203, Kurtöp 'is another example of a tonal language that also has word-level stress', stress on the first syllable (obligatory tone, possible complex onset/long vowel, longer duration). Dzala treated only for sound changes/lexicon (pp. 53-54); no Dzala stress statement. p. 47: Lu 1986 = 'Cuona Memba (actually dialects of Dzala and Dakpa, according to van Driem 2001: 914-915)'; Genetti 2009 HLS-15 talk on Dzala.
